newsitem.title: JAPAN: JAPAN OTC STOCKS SINK ON DULL ECONOMY, OUTLOOK GRIM.
newsitem.headline: JAPAN OTC STOCKS SINK ON DULL ECONOMY, OUTLOOK GRIM.

text.p: The gloom gathering over Japan's economy and the absence of Japan's biggest brokerage from the market are dragging down the Japanese over-the-counter (OTC) stock index, and brokers say there is no respite in sight.

"The OTC firms are mostly small domestic firms dependent on the state of the economy," Akihiro Naemura, strategist at Okasan Securities, said. "With the economic outlook gradually getting bleaker, contrary to earlier hopes, there is little reason for investors to buy."

On Monday, the OTC fell for the 31st consecutive session, dropping 10.47 points, or 0.97 percent, to end at 1,067.55. It was down 1.92 points, or 0.18 percent, at 1,065.63 in mid-afternoon trade on Tuesday.
The index, which consists of many small firms and retailers, has been on a downward trend since the beginning of the year and nearly dropped below the 1,000 mark in April.
It managed a bounce from the April 16 closing low of 1,033.86, but resumed its slide in late June and market sources say there is little hope for a rebound in the near future.
"OTC stocks have fallen to the point where there are many bargains," said Mikio Takada, general manager at Nikko Securities. "But no one wants OTC shares at the moment, even at these low prices."

Brokers said that investors, whose nerves have been rattled by recent grim industrial production data and signs of slackening sales in consumer goods such as cars and computers, are not likely to return to OTC stocks until they are convinced that the economy is back on track.

"The Nikkei average was buoyed in recent sessions by global blue-chips, shares of firms that can make profits abroad and are not effected significantly by domestic matters," said Sanyo Securities general manager Mitsuru Hayashino. "There aren't many such issues on the OTC market and investors pass them by."
Brokers said that the temporary exclusion of Nomura Securities Co from the market as a penalty for its role in a racketeer payoff scandal was also stifling activity.
After issues are registered for trade, lead managers often look after the shares and provide liquidity when needed.
"Liquidity is not very high to begin with in OTC shares and with the main standard-bearer Nomura on the sidelines, it is definitely a minus," said D.E. Shaw research analyst Richard May.
Brokers said that private investors who play the OTC market knew what would happen when penalties were imposed against Nomura and cashed in their positions early.
They have diverted their funds to market newcomers such as Fuji Television Network Inc, which was listed on the first section of the Tokyo Stock Exchange last week.

"Private investors won't come back until things get better, probably after Nomura returns to the market in December," a broker at a "Big Four" brokerage said. Among the penalties slapped on Nomura by the Finance Ministry were orders to suspend stock dealing on its own account until the end of the year.
Also weighing on the OTC market is a rise in the number of new issues, adding to the supply of shares despite the sputtering economy.
Industry sources say that the number of firms making their debut on the OTC market is set to hit a record high of 140 in 1997, exceeding the previous high of 137 in 1995.

Beset by the unclear economic outlook, low liquidity and fears of oversupply, broker said that the only glimmer of hope was that companies' interim earnings, scheduled to be released in October and November, would show an improvement.

"There is a chance that earnings may show an improvement on a year-on-year basis, which could ease fears over their performance," said Masanao Kurimoto, a senior analyst at Yamaichi Research Institute.
"But the leaders, in this case, would be firms such as Shohkoh Fund & Co Ltd which adhere to global standards and have a high market value, not necessarily the more domestic issues."
